sn12.66:1.7: _Sammasa_ only appears in one other case in early Pali, at [thag1.23:1.3](). The root is _mas_ (“to rub”), suggesting the idea of examining with the fingers or “to probe”.
sn12.66:3.6: “Attachment” is _upadhi_, which is both the things of the world to which we cling, and the inner clinging (see [snp1.2](), [mn105:28.2.]()). The Jains defined _upadhi_ similarly (Tattvārthasūtra 9.26). The dominant meaning in Sanskrit is “fraud”, which perhaps informs the Buddhist sense: the things we attach to give a false sense of security. Here it plays the role of “grasping” (_upādāna_).
sn12.66:13.10: The drinks are _surā_ (beer), _dadhimaṇḍaka_ (buttermilk or whey), _maṭṭhaloṇikā_ (salted whey or sour cream, i.e. lassi), and _loṇasovīraka_ (salted infusion of fermented barley and herbs). These correspond with drinks mentioned, along with others, in the Cāraka Saṁhita as _surā_, _mastu_ (Hindi _maṭṭhā_), _dadhimaṇḍa_, and _sauvīraka_. These were fermented drinks used as purgatives, and some or all were also recreational liquors. | _Ayaṁ surāpipāsitā pānīyena vā vinetuṁ_ seems corrupt, read: _ayaṁ pipāsā surāpānīyena vā vinetuṁ_ (“to dispel this thirst by a drink of beer”). | _Loṇasovīraka_ is allowed as medicine ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj3:5.33.14](), [pli-tv-kd6:16.3.1](); preparation methods are given in Suśruta Saṁhitā 1.44 and commentary to Pj 3). It probably originated in Sovīra ([dn19:36.6]()). Sanskrit just has _sauvīraka_ but Cāraka Saṁhita 3.1.18 says it can be drunk with salt; salted drinks are still popular in India. It was a great favorite of the hard-partying women of Madra, who, it was said, would sooner part with husband or son than a drop of _sauvīraka_ (Mahābhārata 8.30). | The last phrase is corrupt, read _ahitāya dukkhāya_ following PTS and Bodhi.
